thread.title: Debt Could Hurt Netflix, GM, and CBS Stock, Bernstein Says

author: Barron's
title: Debt Could Hurt Netflix, GM, and CBS Stock, Bernstein Says
text:
Photograph by Evans/Three Lions/Getty Images What do CBS (ticker: CBS), McDonald's ( MCD ), and General Motors ( GM ) have in common? Bernstein strategists say all three are the type of companies that stock investors should avoid this year.
The issue: their balance sheets. All three companies have relatively high amounts of total debt, compared with their pretax profits, and are rated at the bottom of the investment-grade scale.
Inigo Fraser-Jenkins and his team are certainly not the first to point out the growing number of companies at the lowest end of the investment-grade scale (BBB+, BBB, and BBB-). While analysts have been warning about the risk of more BBB-rated bonds, others say those concerns are overwrought as low-rated companies like AT&T ( T ) shore up their balance sheets so credit-rating firms don't downgrade them to junk.
Yet the Bernstein strategists take a different approach in their analysis. They are more concerned about equities-specifically, the near-record share of companies with low credit ratings in U.S. and European stock markets. High-rated companies make up about half of the U.S. stock market today , they write in a Jan. 30 note, while such companies made up more than 80% of the market 20 years ago.
What drove this change, and what does it mean for investors?
Read more: The Biggest Risk Facing the Economy Right Now, According to Bond King Jeffrey Gundlach
It is difficult to describe what exactly caused the deterioration in credit, but easy central-bank policies certainly didn't hurt. When rates are low, companies can cheaply issue debt and use that cash to boost shareholder returns with buybacks, dividends, or deals.
As for investors, Fraser-Jenkins and his team write that the party might be over for shareholders looking for debt-financed payouts. While companies with weak balance sheets have outperformed in recent years, that trend could reverse itself now that global central banks are starting to raise interest rates.
"Having high leverage was rewarded in a market supported by QE, not least because buybacks expanded," the Bernstein team writes. "But we think that times are now changing."
Companies with high-quality balance sheets and higher credit ratings should outperform as economic growth starts to slow, the strategists say. They found that the shares of high-rated U.S. companies outperform shares of junk-rated companies during recessions. In Europe, high-quality company shares outperform during recessions and when economic growth is slowing.
Bernstein expects credit spreads-the bond market's measure of corporate default risk-to continue to widen. And that increase should be "a catalyst for high balance sheet quality companies to outperform."
The strategists' list of high-quality U.S. stocks includes Alphabet ( GOOGL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), and Visa (V), while their low-quality stocks include Netflix (NFLX), Ford Motor (F), and, somewhat confusingly, Apple (AAPL). (Apple executives have said the company plans to reduce its net debt to zero.)
Still, there are a couple of problems with Bernstein's broader argument.
First, the market overwhelmingly expects the Federal Reserve to pause raising interest rates for most of this year. And while the Fed could still tighten by shrinking its balance sheet, the market doesn't seem too worried about that. Stocks of low-quality companies have recovered from their brief, sharp underperformance during the late-2018 market volatility.
The credit spreads of BBB-rated bonds have narrowed as well. In other words, investors are demanding less extra yield to own BBB-rated bonds over comparable Treasury bonds.
What's more, credit ratings may not be the best way to gauge balance-sheet quality at this point in the cycle.
https://asset.barrons.com/dj-mg/dice/barrons-staffpicks-2d590600-c862-4394-b9d3-66b48c376d60/inset.json
As mentioned above, many BBB-rated companies are reducing their leverage levels to defend their investment-grade ratings. AT&T, for example, said last year it would use all its spare cash to pay back bondholders and reduce debt levels. On Tuesday, Verizon Communications (VZ) focused so much on debt reduction in its earnings call that its bond spreads tightened even though shares fell, according to Bank of America Merrill Lynch. And Advance Auto Parts (AAP) announced it will redeem $300 million of 2020 bonds "to maintain an investment grade rating."
Many A-rated companies, on the other hand, are still adding debt. IBM (IBM), for example, could take on significant debt to finance its planned $34 billion acquisition of Red Hat (RHT).
Investors may still want to buy shares of high-quality companies at this late point of the economic expansion. Even so, they should do their homework to make sure the company's credit rating matches its credit quality.
Write to Alexandra Scaggs at alexandra.scaggs@barrons.com
